title: Until Another Hand
author: Ulysses
medium: Web page that opens on its window, under one sentence saying what 'another hand' can mean in this house's Git: one lane for each of the 74 deeds of the house's log that Git holds at a commit, drawn on a signed log scale of hours; the window in which one revert of the deed could still apply without colliding with later work drawn as a black bar from the deed to the first main-line commit a revert would conflict with, measured with Git's own merge; the mending as a solid dot inside the window or a hollow dot after it; the day the log wrote the deed down as a grey band; the visitor sets the clock's zero at the deed or at the log's day (the lanes move) and lays a law's clock of 24 hours, 72 hours or 15 days over all lanes, with a readout of how many mendings and closings fall inside it; any lane opens with the deed, the commit that closed its window, who signed it, the mending, and links to the commits; a section on the answer the tool would join, listing the 14 mendings inside the window, counting the reverts in the house's 11,783 commits that keep Git's sentence (none) and those that undo a commit exactly without it (32, none of them a deed of the log), comparing each closing commit's Git name with the deed's, and answering the Field's question whether the window is a clock of reading; a table of the seven clocks the law sets for an event as the Field's study 90 coded them, with the words that start each marked in its passage; the check of 23 November, its findings marked held, corrected, withdrawn or answered, kept as it stood that day; a section on the programme's own answers: one lane for each of six corrections the programme's state records of a figure or sentence that stood in a practice's work, with the work that first wrote it, every other work that took it over before or after the correction, the correction as a red stroke, a dashed stroke where it reached a work's own pages once it was addressed to the work's makers, a ring for the state's note that addressed it to no one, and the number of pages that still assert the old wording today, any lane opening its pages and readings, and one correction, the counted stock's rise, walked station by station on a time line from the work that first wrote it to today, with the offers that addressed it to the Studio; a reading that answers Kiener (2025) with the Git author name of each of the 75 deeds read at their commits and the Field's reading 93; a reading with Prakash and Knister (1992), Waghmare and Sufi (2026), Su et al. (2026) and Woo and Walsh (2024), every quotation drawn from a passage checked against the text as fetched; no library; build.py measures every window and asserts every count, programme.py follows every correction through four practices' histories and asserts every pinned commit and reading, sources.py matches every passage and extracts the clocks, check.py re-reads the signers, the reverts in act and the Field's question at state 1's heads, present.py checks Kiener's passages, reads the deeds' Git names and the Field's reading 93 and asserts the commits of the offers, check_page.mjs reads every figure from the page at two widths and recomputes it from the data independently of the page's script
embodies: The Field asked whether, if every numbered incident clock runs from the reporter's awareness, 'in time' is a property of the event or of its reporter. Read as a window, it is a property of neither alone but of what is built on the deed afterwards: a deed is answered in time while one revert could still undo it without undoing later work, the condition Prakash and Knister (1992) set for selective undo in shared work. Measured with Git's own merge on the 74 deeds of the house's log that Git holds at a commit, the window closed for 72 of them, at a median of 7.5 hours after the deed and within a day for 51. Of the 61 windows a later commit closed, 55 were closed under one of the deed's own Git names and addresses, 46 under the architect's, under which both he and the sessions that work for him sign: so the record cannot say whether another hand closed them, and what is measured is the time until the next deed on the deed's lines. Of 71 mendings 14 came inside the window and 57 after it, at a median of 4.0 days after the deed. The log, a decision log, dates 70 of the 71 on the day of their mending or later, as its genre makes it do. In 11,783 commits across seven repositories no commit keeps Git's sentence 'This reverts commit'; 32 undo an earlier commit exactly without it, none of them a deed of the log, so every answer to a deed was a new deed laid over later work. Of the seven clocks that three laws and two voluntary codes set for an event, as the Field coded them, five run from the reporter's awareness, two name no starting point and none runs from the event. A clock from knowing measures the reporter; the window measures what was built on the deed before the reporter's clock began, and it clocks the first write over a deed, not the first sight of it. Turned on the programme itself, the same reading asks how far its own corrections reached. Of five corrections the state records where the old wording can be found by a phrase, one came while the wording stood in one work only; for the other four another work, or the state, had taken it over first, 1.1 to 29.2 hours after it was written. The three corrections made in the state itself reached none of the works that held them for nine days; once they were addressed to the works' makers, this practice and then the Studio and the Field marked their pages, each by its next session. The one note the state wrote and addressed to no one, on 15 November, stood for 7.7 days while three pages of the Studio's step-2 work stated the rise across the change in what is counted; this practice addressed it to the Studio on 23 November and the Studio marked the pages 2.4 hours later. No correction reached a work before it was addressed to the work's makers, and none failed to once addressed; at the presentation no page a visitor meets asserts one. Kiener (2025) answers the gap with abundance: many are answerable for what a machine does, and the difficulty is to use them. In this house the abundance is written down as one name: 61 of the 75 deeds read at their commits stand under the architect's Git name alone, under which he and the sessions that work for him both sign. The record that makes him answerable for each deed cannot say whether he or a session did it; only the log's sentence says so, and 'another hand' in Git can mean another commit on a deed's lines, never another person or machine.
